![](images/01/019f0f9f83ddf323d543d109677335cb3ae72a200baf834453a0eca16a9353ba.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/d2/d222e86f6af7c3ed2b35711114c9062d6f0c9b0f2551aa44cac33318c6e5813f.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,x+2\le y\le \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\le y\le x+2\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{x+2}^{{x}^{2}/2+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}/2+2}^{x+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-266a83b4-e89e-5341-ae78-39b530317ac4" :question/id #uuid "266a83b4-e89e-5341-ae78-39b530317ac4" :question/math-academy-id "q-132296" :question/problem "Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=\frac{3x}{2}+6,$ $y=-3x-3$ and $y=0.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions." :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region.

![](images/8d/8dad5cdaa9fdcaf0293773c53a0b5ab58d7d98aea0099af0a9ba616e72759129.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/a0/a0b5bfe05214df5f59a563677bd6b4f7dfd85be4d8e27fd4d7b31f87a679cd2b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-4\le x\le -2,\,0\le y\le \frac{3x}{2}+6\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le -1,\,0\le y\le -3x-3\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{-2}{\int }_{0}^{3x/2+6}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{\int }_{0}^{-3x-3}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-467e7482-236e-50bd-9069-2e1ac24cf7f7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id ![](images/8a/8a46756cd4842caf7977ef72ae05912a635843a06382b21136362455a94369e4.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.   Notice that we're using that $x=3-{y}^{2}$ can be split into $y=\pm \sqrt{3-x}.$ 

![](images/43/43da7a61d7a4bff15274cdacbf1f3265c097edb8740583c69463460467f8100f.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 2,\,1-x\le y\le \sqrt{3-x}\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 3,\,-\sqrt{3-x}\le y\le \sqrt{3-x}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{1-x}^{\sqrt{3-x}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{-\sqrt{3-x}}^{\sqrt{3-x}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-54e9c707-1747-52ad-abb8-366afb9bc3dd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/0e/0e69b1cb480b87216273db4336adff57cbf9d9bc450aac4b0cdb58b1ae63f6f7.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-3\le x\le 0,\,-\frac{2x}{3}\le y\le \frac{x}{3}+3\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,\frac{4x}{3}\le y\le \frac{x}{3}+3\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}{\int }_{-2x/3}^{x/3+3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{4x/3}^{x/3+3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186268861 :question/worked-solution "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-x & \,⟹\,x=-y \\ y=6-4x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4} \\ y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/08/08237d1ca2e01d0cf620dfa06a4265d8053b7ee34d0b65036aad7d5734726e1c.png)

 

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/c7/c756dc7924fc4c116601da907eb3b767b8a40647e063c146dad83b0ea660933b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y/2}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186394366 :question/worked-solution "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\sqrt{x-2}+1 & \,⟹\,x=(y-1)^{2}+2 \\ y=2-\frac{1}{2}x & \,⟹\,x=4-2y \\ y=8-2x & \,⟹\,x=4-\frac{1}{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/3f/3f8e3ccfeac236d7fe9a502f599c61c404607a55ae809ec142019a3f881e1568.png)

  

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/31/3148cb0f499564db9cbfd6b635fef81dc47298789241af4a243c32dbf4dc8247.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,4-2y\le x\le 4-\frac{1}{2}y\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,(y-1)^{2}+2\le x\le 4-\frac{1}{2}y\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{4-2y}^{4-y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{(y-1)^{2}+2}^{4-y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-94516772-c0e6-5471-a227-05c6f1da1b17" :question/id #uuid "94516772-c0e6-5471-a227-05c6f1da1b17" :question/math-academy-id "q-132380" :question/problem "![](images/48/4826bc628c1bd8f4293fd5fbf90bf9155658c15336c2c9e86a5e7678dfcf1ca3.png)

Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions." :question/worked-solution "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-x & \,⟹\,x=-y \\ y=x+4 & \,⟹\,x=y-4\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/17/17d3ceabf3cd7a052398d8d12b7963c5ca64356605554e3ff43c21c7321e45de.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y-4\le x\le -y\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,-y\le x\le y-4\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y-4}^{-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{-y}^{y-4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ $y=2x,$ and $y=\frac{(2x+2)}{3},$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions." :question/worked-solution "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{2y} \\ y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y=\frac{2x+2}{3} & \,⟹\,x=\frac{3y-2}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/63/63848a26cff0641ac83c73e809028852697212ce64a8cb954815d514922721a1.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{2y}\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,\frac{3y-2}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{2y}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y/2}^{\sqrt{2y}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{(3y-2)/2}^{\sqrt{2y}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d14fe408-e710-5a6c-9dc2-c17893127e06"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={e}^{x} & \,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,x={e}^{y} \\ y=1+e-x & \,⟹\,x=1+e-y \\ y=1-x & \,⟹\,x=1-y\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/4d/4df7cf2f33520a80270341d4a40b4a83d9f3c11ed8adb69fe1131a42bcd61d5a.png)

    

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1-y\le x\le {e}^{y}\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le e,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡y\le x\le 1+e-y\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-y}^{{e}^{y}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}^{1+e-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186268864 :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/33/33a38da74b282f0ec1fb2fae9cb155feb2a5fd39128c7607b80c6b84fedd29b4.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,x-1\le y\le 3-x\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,3-x\le y\le x-1\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{x-1}^{3-x}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{3-x}^{x-1}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{x-1}^{3-x}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{3-x}^{x-1}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[(3-x)^{2}-(x-1)^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}[(x-1)^{2}-(3-x)^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(8-4x)\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}(4x-8)\text{d}x \\  & =(8x-2{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{2}+(2{x}^{2}-8x){|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =8(2-1)-2({2}^{2}-{1}^{2})+2({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})-8(4-2) \\  & =8-6+24-16 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351419 :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/64/648121ff2a676f6a472a6e221dffe813eca55f914aed0ca9a285bb0d4cd81ab3.png)

   

As a result, we get 

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le 3\},

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}4xy\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}4xy\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[2x{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}{[2x{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2x(9-1)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}2x(9-0)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}16x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}18x\,\text{d}x \\  & =8{x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{2}+9{x}^{2}{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =8(4-0)+9(9-4) \\  & =77.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351418 :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/2f/2fcb30778db2f051a7a819ae701808af59ac18d27c25a9c57ce678caa6c3ee3b.png)

$$

and

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2x\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2x\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2x\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2x[-x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2x[x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(-2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{-1}^{0}+{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =((0-(-\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{4}))+((\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{4})-0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129616 :question/problem "${∬}_{|x|+|y|\le 1}\,\,{e}^{x+y}\,dA=$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a sketch of our region.

![](images/4f/4f4e38950d36bf77ce4b2a907f07b3f9c4b40837729ef644f37ecfbd921aec8a.png)

  

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{|x|+|y|\le 1}{e}^{x+y}\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}{e}^{x+y}\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}{e}^{x+y}\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-x-1}^{x+1}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{-x+1}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[{e}^{x+y}]_{-x-1}^{x+1}\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}[{e}^{x+y}]_{x-1}^{-x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({e}^{2x+1}-{e}^{-1})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}(e-{e}^{2x-1})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{e}^{2x+1}}{2}-{e}^{-1}x]}_{-1}^{0}+{[ex-\frac{{e}^{2x-1}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{e}{2}-(\frac{{e}^{-1}}{2}+{e}^{-1})]+[(e-\frac{e}{2})+\frac{{e}^{-1}}{2}] \\  & =e-{e}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186127177 :answer-field/correct "answer-830d9a09-4b3d-5488-ab8b-7407c02fb4fe" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7da24e9f-953b-5b8d-9fb3-433072fccab1" "answer-d10e18e2-81c4-5858-b24a-9e24eac04a78" "answer-bf4fcd37-0cd2-54cf-8269-3de8bbb9ae1f" "answer-5426c146-fb3d-500e-b01e-5ede41135cc4" "answer-830d9a09-4b3d-5488-ab8b-7407c02fb4fe"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7da24e9f-953b-5b8d-9fb3-433072fccab1" :answer/id #uuid "7da24e9f-953b-5b8d-9fb3-433072fccab1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(e-{e}^{-1})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d10e18e2-81c4-5858-b24a-9e24eac04a78" :answer/id #uuid "d10e18e2-81c4-5858-b24a-9e24eac04a78" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{e-{e}^{-1}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bf4fcd37-0cd2-54cf-8269-3de8bbb9ae1f" :answer/id #uuid "bf4fcd37-0cd2-54cf-8269-3de8bbb9ae1f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{e}{2}-{e}^{-1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5426c146-fb3d-500e-b01e-5ede41135cc4" :answer/id #uuid "5426c146-fb3d-500e-b01e-5ede41135cc4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e-\frac{{e}^{-1}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-830d9a09-4b3d-5488-ab8b-7407c02fb4fe" :answer/id #uuid "830d9a09-4b3d-5488-ab8b-7407c02fb4fe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e-{e}^{-1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186323935 :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into three type II regions ${D}_{1},$ ${D}_{2},$ and ${D}_{3},$ as shown below.

![](images/b5/b58fc3909d5be467999053336f67d41b88b43c984208c60f3d46ee8b7479df58.png)

As a result, we get 

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,-2\le x\le -1\},
$$

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le x\le 2\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{3}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,-2\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}{x}^{2}y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}{x}^{2}y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{3}}{x}^{2}y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{y\text{ }\,{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{-1}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{y\text{ }\,{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{y\text{ }\,{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7y}{3}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7y}{3}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{16y}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot \frac{7}{3}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}+\frac{16}{3}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =\frac{71}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130400 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the double integral  

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 2(x+y)\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the finite region bounded by the lines $x=0, \, y=1, \, y=2, \, y=3-x,$ and $y=x.$ How do we proceed?

To evaluate an integral like this, we carry out the following steps: 

**Step 1.** Sketch the region $D$. This allows us to determine the precise set-up of our integral. 

In this example, we obtain the following:

![](images/0a/0a90a4f377327f5293308f1e08ac6596f1c27b9bd47a614d6d7cb1c5dbfec33c.png)

**Step 2.** Split (if necessary) the region $D$ into several type I or II regions.

From the diagram above, we see that our region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as follows.

![](images/a9/a93e1a0a0a7f9c104cb5d380b2a7ff98d6712ef0d2d67b74130da5dcf1701443.png)

 

So, we get

$$
D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq 1, \quad 1 \leq y \leq 2\big\}
$$

and

$$
D_2= \{(x,y)\: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 3/2,  \quad  x \leq y \leq 3-x\}
$$

**Step 3.** Set up and evaluate the integral using the additivity property of double integrals. We recall the following fact:

*If $D$ is the union of two sub-regions, $D_1, D_2$, that don't overlap then,*

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A.
$$

So, finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}2(x+y)\text{ }dy\,dx+{\int }_{1}^{3/2}{\int }_{x}^{3-x}2(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

 However, a trinomial is *not always* cubic (see, for example, statement I). 

 So, some trinomials are cubic.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-68adcac4-f714-5f55-81da-9c003d947562"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-68adcac4-f714-5f55-81da-9c003d947562" :answer-field/id #uuid "68adcac4-f714-5f55-81da-9c003d947562" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8efd74f5-cafb-5856-a477-190813a8a4ff" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c9db9c56-7c9d-5fbd-9ab7-859523a2dbc1" "answer-7ef2bd94-3507-5818-a8e2-21b4e3d5daaa" "answer-031cfe8a-aedb-5c47-85b8-b78d424c9253" "answer-8efd74f5-cafb-5856-a477-190813a8a4ff" "answer-4cb13528-7dc2-5e8c-81d3-76237471c1a9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c9db9c56-7c9d-5fbd-9ab7-859523a2dbc1" :answer/id #uuid "c9db9c56-7c9d-5fbd-9ab7-859523a2dbc1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ef2bd94-3507-5818-a8e2-21b4e3d5daaa" :answer/id #uuid "7ef2bd94-3507-5818-a8e2-21b4e3d5daaa" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-031cfe8a-aedb-5c47-85b8-b78d424c9253" :answer/id #uuid "031cfe8a-aedb-5c47-85b8-b78d424c9253" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8efd74f5-cafb-5856-a477-190813a8a4ff" :answer/id #uuid "8efd74f5-cafb-5856-a477-190813a8a4ff" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4cb13528-7dc2-5e8c-81d3-76237471c1a9" :answer/id #uuid "4cb13528-7dc2-5e8c-81d3-76237471c1a9" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-298a3ab5-9f3b-5907-82bb-2239de27222c" :question/id #uuid "298a3ab5-9f3b-5907-82bb-2239de27222c" :question/math-academy-id "q-152438" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The product of $7x$ and $3{x}^{2}$ is a binomial.

II. The product of $4x$ and $5$ is a monomial.

III. The product of two monomials is **always** a binomial." :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
(7x)\times (3{x}^{2})=21{x}^{3},
$$

which is *not* a binomial (it's a monomial).

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
(4x)\times (5)=20x,
$$

which is a monomial.

- Statement III is false. There are products of two monomials that are not binomials (see, for example, statement I and II).

In fact, the product of two monomials is *never* a binomial.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-62c88c7f-5c96-5f04-a40f-dca9bee2c854"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-62c88c7f-5c96-5f04-a40f-dca9bee2c854" :answer-field/id #uuid "62c88c7f-5c96-5f04-a40f-dca9bee2c854" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5cb50a14-8d14-5abf-bbba-8ffff9b40b1f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0ae009f5-4ad8-554c-9afe-f7df0d60df6c" "answer-ec85cf8b-2ad9-57c7-abee-ddf2ba3c9e29" "answer-d6d1b1b3-57ce-5b6f-aeae-962b95ce3397" "answer-5cb50a14-8d14-5abf-bbba-8ffff9b40b1f" "answer-e11a5ec7-6258-52b7-931d-7cf5782a0e9c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0ae009f5-4ad8-554c-9afe-f7df0d60df6c" :answer/id #uuid "0ae009f5-4ad8-554c-9afe-f7df0d60df6c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ec85cf8b-2ad9-57c7-abee-ddf2ba3c9e29" :answer/id #uuid "ec85cf8b-2ad9-57c7-abee-ddf2ba3c9e29" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d6d1b1b3-57ce-5b6f-aeae-962b95ce3397" :answer/id #uuid "d6d1b1b3-57ce-5b6f-aeae-962b95ce3397" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5cb50a14-8d14-5abf-bbba-8ffff9b40b1f" :answer/id #uuid "5cb50a14-8d14-5abf-bbba-8ffff9b40b1f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e11a5ec7-6258-52b7-931d-7cf5782a0e9c" :answer/id #uuid "e11a5ec7-6258-52b7-931d-7cf5782a0e9c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186055997 :tutorial/content "Polynomials with one, two, or three terms have special names.

- A polynomial with one term is called a **monomial**. For example:
 

$$
1, \qquad y,	\qquad	2x^3,	\qquad	5a^{4}
$$

However, the following expressions are not monomials because they can't be called polynomials:
 

$$
\dfrac{1}{y},	\qquad	5t^{-1},	\qquad \sqrt{x}, \qquad 	2z^{1/4}
$$

- A polynomial with two terms is called a **binomial**. For example:

$$
x+3,	\qquad	7n^2 +n,	\qquad	p^{32} -1
$$

- A polynomial with three terms is called a **trinomial**. For example:
 

$$
z^2 -z +1,	\qquad	x^3 -2x -1,	\qquad	2c^{4} - 3c^{3} +4c^2
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186055998 :tutorial/content "Each type of polynomial of degree between $0$ and $5$ has a specific name. These are shown in the table below.

| Degree | Name | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | Constant | $7$ |
| $1$ | Linear | $3x + 2$ |
| $2$ | Quadratic | $2x^2 - 6x + 1$ |
| $3$ | Cubic | $x^3 + 4x^2 + 9x$ |
| $4$ | Quartic | $3x^4 - 5x^2$ |
| $5$ | Quintic | $7x^5 + 3x^4 - x^4 + x - 6$ |

We can combine these with the names we learned earlier. 

For example:

- $2x+1$ is a *linear binomial* because its degree equals $1,$ and it has $2$ terms.

- $x^2$ is a *quadratic monomial* because its degree equals $2,$ and it has $1$ term.

- $2x^3+x+1$ is a *cubic trinomial* because its degree equals $3,$ and it has $3$ terms.

If a polynomial contains more than three terms, then we refer to it by its degree only.

For example:

- $x^3+2x^2+x-1$ is a *cubic polynomial.*

- $x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1$ is a *quartic polynomial.*" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054924 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198390 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/id #uuid "fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-162559" :question/problem "![](images/80/804976bf326ed561ff8e7b4f5a6c65361039a686a4449edfdf8e6f497ee5cbda.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/de/de9eb8381df05d2d5e6222a51b0ccbc5729e522df94a4aace570881d1226a1ca.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xz]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}-z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}z-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[x]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =(-1)+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2652e0ca-544c-51d5-827f-9347b3d96ac0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186326747 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 \\ 20 & 8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8+4\text{i} & -4 \\ 20 & 8+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-8+4\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 20{x}_{1}+(8+4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=4\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}=\frac{(-2+\text{i})(-2-\text{i})}{(1)(1)}=5.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351202 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 2 \\ -3 & -2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\sqrt{2}\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-2}{2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}}=\frac{-2(2-\sqrt{2}\text{i})}{6}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{i}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351255 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 5 \\ -4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 5 \\ -4 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+4\text{i})(-2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186272074 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133740 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-da278c6f-6480-5739-b071-7c465347a792" "question-bcb80b5f-d39a-5f5e-9109-13ded54ba26d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133513 :question/worked-solution "To work out $\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^3,$ we multiply $\dfrac{3}{5}$ by itself and then multiply the result by $\dfrac{3}{5}$ again:

For example, to "cube $2$", we need to multiply $2$ by $2$ to make $4,$ and then multiply this result by $2$ once more. We write the "cube of $2$" as $2^3,$ so we have

$$
2^3 = \underbrace{2\cdot 2}_{\large 4} \cdot 2 = 4 \cdot 2 = 8.
$$

We would then say that "the cube of $2$ is $8$". We could also say "$2$ cubed equals $8$".

The number ${\color{blue}3}$ in the expression $2^{\color{blue}3}$ is called the power (or exponent).

The act of cubing a number can be represented geometrically. For example, let's start by representing the number $2$ with the following collection of two items:

![](images/b6/b6a13017dcbcf25a66ab576189690e8879a4ccbb3c4c5562b129f4dd15af4e85.png)

Then we can picture $2^3$ by creating a bigger shape (called a **cube**) with length, width and height all equal to $2\mathbin{:}$

![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png)

There are $8$ items in total in our big cube (one little cube is hiding behind the others), indicating that $2^3=8.$

Clearly, $1^3=1\cdot1\cdot1={\color{blue}1}.$ The next few first basic cubes are shown below:

| $2^3=2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2={\color{blue}8}$ | $3^3=3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3={\color{blue}27}$ | $4^3=4 \cdot 4 \cdot 4={\color{blue}64}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png) | ![](images/cb/cb3171dc7f7a2e9838c3e8b46c3ce385be28624b4474391b9bb211b5a599fa55.png) | ![](images/65/6546ffc5df407b29df601252e1f5afa8e01b17dca5c7169a6321d550d86255c3.png) |

The cubes of our usual counting numbers are called **cube numbers** or **perfect cubes**. We can write them as follows:

$$
1^3, 2^3, 3^3, 4^3, 5^3, 6^3, \ldots \qquad \text{or} \qquad {\color{blue}1}, {\color{blue}8}, {\color{blue}27}, {\color{blue}64}, {\color{blue}125}, {\color{blue}216}, \ldots
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135184 :tutorial/content "Cubing a negative number *always* results in another negative number.

This is because a negative times a negative gives a positive value, and then a positive times a negative is a negative again:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,{{(-)\,\cdot \,(-)}_{⏟}}_{(+)}\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(+)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(-)\end{aligned}
$$

For example,

$$
({\color{red}-5})^3 = \underbrace{({\color{red}-5}) \cdot ({\color{red}-5})}_{\large {\color{blue}25}} \cdot ({\color{red}-5}) = {\color{blue}25} \cdot ({\color{red}-5}) = {\color{red}-125}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134039 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186123164 :answer-field/choices 17592186123168] [:db/retract 17592186123164 :answer-field/choices 17592186123169] [:db/retract 17592186123164 :answer-field/choices 17592186123165] [:db/retract 17592186123164 :answer-field/choices 17592186123167] [:db/retract 17592186125060 :question/answer-fields 17592186122960] {:db/id 17592186124551 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" "question-e9c15a3d-862e-553a-bd17-8b80866daf10" "question-63615617-5b80-58c9-8714-0059cfaa1f62"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124535 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e91960f2-bae8-5967-8997-6021ee7e8a3f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" :question/id #uuid "ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" :question/math-academy-id "q-140315" :question/problem "$$

$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 8 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-8) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -5)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -20) & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)(\lambda +4)(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda -5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=5$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-4}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-4})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=5.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{5}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-5I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 5\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -8 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+8{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5.$ So,

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{5})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-4})+\text{dim}({V}_{5})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, a corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e4a53fb3-00cc-58aa-aebb-3f7e25363f55"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=5$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=2.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{2}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{2})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=5.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{5}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-5I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & -7 & 3\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & -7 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). This implies that we will have $3-2=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{5})=1.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is *not* diagonalizable, since 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{2})+\text{dim}({V}_{5})=1+1=2\ne 3.\,\times

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=7.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{7}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{7})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{4}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-4I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 7\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{4})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{7})+\text{dim}({V}_{4})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, the corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries of the main diagonal. Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=12$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-6$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=12.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{12}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=12$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{12})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-6.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-6}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-6)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-6)I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 12 & 0 \\ -3 & 6 & -6\end{aligned}]-(-6)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 18 & 0 \\ -3 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ -9 & 18 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-6.$ So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-6})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{12})+\text{dim}({V}_{-6})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, the corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$

A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 6 & -6 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & a & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & b & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $D={P}^{-1}AP$ is a diagonalization of the matrix $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

The second column of $P$ corresponds to $\lambda =1.$ Computing $A-\lambda I,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 6 & -6 & 7\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 6 & -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}={x}_{2}-{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Comparing this with the second column of $P,$ we deduce that ${x}_{2}=0.$ Now, setting ${x}_{3}=-1$ and substituting our values for ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ into the general solution, we obtain the following: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=-\frac{1}{1}=-1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ffba39de-be3f-50d3-b059-2377c3c0d428"] :db/ensure $$

$$

$$

Finally, position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$ is obtained by substituting $t=0$ into the equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2+(0),4+4(0),-1+3(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,4,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨2,0,2⟩\times ⟨1,4,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-8i+2j+8k \\  & =⟨-8,2,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =⟨-15,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨2,3,1⟩+w⟨-3,-2,3⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130 \\ ⟨2-3w,3-2w,1+3w⟩\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130 \\ -8(2-3w)+2(3-2w)+8(1+3w) & =130 \\ -16+24w+6-4w+8+24w & =130 \\ 44w & =132 \\ w & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=3$ into the equation of the line:

$$

$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(-7,-3,10).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d9d0e6f8-2892-55f4-a237-affcef970729"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d9d0e6f8-2892-55f4-a237-affcef970729" :answer-field/id #uuid "d9d0e6f8-2892-55f4-a237-affcef970729" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b2c22028-564a-5c89-ab16-c9763fcf688a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-384678c4-4350-5113-9f0f-32d8e2cf6110" "answer-b2c22028-564a-5c89-ab16-c9763fcf688a" "answer-35e34ef5-0c0f-566b-94a8-9376d485a3d4" "answer-92098877-886b-53fa-a483-755c30d71d2e" "answer-c36ccfc7-634d-5201-b479-3d9288da2e97"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-384678c4-4350-5113-9f0f-32d8e2cf6110" :answer/id #uuid "384678c4-4350-5113-9f0f-32d8e2cf6110" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-1,1,4)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b2c22028-564a-5c89-ab16-c9763fcf688a" :answer/id #uuid "b2c22028-564a-5c89-ab16-c9763fcf688a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-7,-3,10)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-35e34ef5-0c0f-566b-94a8-9376d485a3d4" :answer/id #uuid "35e34ef5-0c0f-566b-94a8-9376d485a3d4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(0,0,0)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92098877-886b-53fa-a483-755c30d71d2e" :answer/id #uuid "92098877-886b-53fa-a483-755c30d71d2e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(10,3,2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c36ccfc7-634d-5201-b479-3d9288da2e97" :answer/id #uuid "c36ccfc7-634d-5201-b479-3d9288da2e97" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "No intersection" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-07e33caa-9650-5834-8d9a-46cc82f723d1" :question/id #uuid "07e33caa-9650-5834-8d9a-46cc82f723d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-108434" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
6x-(3+2x)
$$

In this example, we're subtracting the entire group of terms in parentheses from $6x.$ In such cases, we distribute the negative sign to each term in the parentheses *first* and then simplify by collecting like terms.

Removing the parentheses by distributing the negative sign, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-(3+2x) & = \\ 6x-3-2x & .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-3-2x & = \\ (6x-2x)-3 & = \\ 4x-3 & \end{aligned}
$$

Let's take a look at another example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186189441 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, to subtract a group of terms, we have to apply the distributive law.

For example, let's simplify the following expression:

$$
7-4(y+2)
$$

First, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
7 - \Big[4(y+2)\Big]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
7 - \Big[4y+8\Big].
$$

Now, we proceed as before. Removing the brackets by distributing the negative sign gives

$$
7 - 4y - 8.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}7-4y-8 & = \\ (7-8)-4y & = \\ -1-4y & \end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188467 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124457 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/id #uuid "83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/math-academy-id "q-129409" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$

tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z)\text{ }k \\  & =(1-2xz)\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j-{x}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(\,1-2(1)(2)\,)\text{ }i+2(1)\text{ }j-(1)^{2}k \\  & =-3\,i+2\,j-1\,k \\  & =⟨-3,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-3,2,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b758f2b0-ee02-5c9d-8c7b-99e5dc8caa68"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}z+{z}^{2}y+{y}^{2}x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}z+{z}^{2}y+{y}^{2}x)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}z+{z}^{2}y+{y}^{2}x)\text{ }k \\  & =(2xz+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({z}^{2}+2yx)\text{ }j+({x}^{2}+2zy)k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,-1) & =(2(1)(-1)+{1}^{2})\text{ }i+((-1)^{2}+2(1)(1))\text{ }j+({1}^{2}+2(-1)(1))k \\  & =-\,i+3\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,3,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-1,3,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ -(x-1)+3(y-1)-(z+1) & =0 \\ -x+3y-z-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bd5c8610-318e-58b9-8590-725b9e0fa2c5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

the surface $x{y}^{2}+6=z{x}^{2}.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(-2,-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2}+6 & =z{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2} & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(-2,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =({y}^{2}-2xz)\text{ }i+2xy\text{ }j-{x}^{2}\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(-2,-1,1) & =((-1)^{2}-2(-2)(1))\text{ }i+2(-2)(-1)\text{ }j-(-2)^{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5\,i+4j-4\,k \\  & =⟨5,4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(-2,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+1,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨5,4,-4⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+1,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ 5(x+2)+4(y+1)-4(z-1) & =0 \\ 5x+4y-4z+18 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f5f7cc0c-f2cb-5ebd-8a19-e3ddc8cdda4a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id the surface $z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz=2+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.$ Given that $n=⟨a,b,c⟩$ is a non-zero normal vector to the surface at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2),$ what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define  $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=2+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)k \\  & =(-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-yz)i+(-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-xz)j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xy)k \\ ∇f(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2) & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{ }i+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-2(\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{ }j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\frac{\pi }{2})(-\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{ }k \\  & =\pi \text{ }i-\pi \text{ }j+(1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4})\text{ }k \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,-\pi ,\,1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨\pi ,\,-\pi ,\,\frac{{\pi }^{2}+4}{4}⟩.$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\pi }{-\pi }=-1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-32ad6879-6146-512a-b9ce-7b997929ffe5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-32ad6879-6146-512a-b9ce-7b997929ffe5" :answer-field/id #uuid "32ad6879-6146-512a-b9ce-7b997929ffe5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0af3f2c2-59c9-5249-a2d8-811877a6ca18" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0af3f2c2-59c9-5249-a2d8-811877a6ca18" "answer-06ddc08d-d22f-5193-bf06-38fb8c7ba7c7" "answer-19987fb0-bc40-51ba-b84d-d8cb0087f00a" "answer-87b7e1f6-b074-5206-8b9b-5827ab7b73bd" "answer-226d0641-c568-50b8-93be-58d7db8760ad"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0af3f2c2-59c9-5249-a2d8-811877a6ca18" :answer/id #uuid "0af3f2c2-59c9-5249-a2d8-811877a6ca18" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-06ddc08d-d22f-5193-bf06-38fb8c7ba7c7" :answer/id #uuid "06ddc08d-d22f-5193-bf06-38fb8c7ba7c7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-19987fb0-bc40-51ba-b84d-d8cb0087f00a" :answer/id #uuid "19987fb0-bc40-51ba-b84d-d8cb0087f00a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-87b7e1f6-b074-5206-8b9b-5827ab7b73bd" :answer/id #uuid "87b7e1f6-b074-5206-8b9b-5827ab7b73bd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-226d0641-c568-50b8-93be-58d7db8760ad" :answer/id #uuid "226d0641-c568-50b8-93be-58d7db8760ad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130327 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to compute the tangent plane to the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k,$ where $k$ is a constant, at some point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0).$ 

As an example, consider the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2 +y^2+z.
$$

 

Suppose that we wish to find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=  (1,1, 2).$ 

Evaluating $f$ at the point $(1,1,2),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = (1)^2 +(1)^2+2 = 4.
$$

 

So, the equation of our level surface is

$$
x^2 +y^2+z = 4.
$$

Now, to find the equation of the tangent plane to this surface at $(1,1,2),$ we can use the following result:

  *Given a hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ and a point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0,y_0,z_0)$ that lies in the domain of $f$, the gradient $\nabla \! f (\mathbf x_0)$ is normal to the tangent plane of the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k$ at the point $\mathbf x_0$*. 

![](images/11/1140e80fbb2efd684311cb7625e5b0be361d6fb951036253f57b9e51234de3ee.png)

       

We can now find the equation of the tangent plane to our level surface.

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $\mathbf x_0 = (1,1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}\,i+{f}_{y}\,j+{f}_{z}\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(1,1,2) & =2(1)\text{ }i+2(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =2\text{ }i+2\text{ }j+k \\  & =⟨2,\,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally,  we write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\nabla f(1,1,2) \cdot \langle x-1, \: y-1, \: z-2 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\langle 2,\:2,\:1\rangle\cdot \langle x-1, y-1, z-2\rangle &= 0\[3pt]
      2(x-1)+ 2(y-1) + (z-2) & =0\
      2x +2y +z -6&=0   
}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129332 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186052018 :answer-field/choices 17592186052019] [:db/retract 17592186052018 :answer-field/choices 17592186052020] [:db/retract 17592186052018 :answer-field/choices 17592186052021] [:db/retract 17592186052887 :answer-field/choices 17592186052888] [:db/retract 17592186052887 :answer-field/choices 17592186052889] [:db/retract 17592186052887 :answer-field/choices 17592186052890] [:db/retract 17592186052887 :answer-field/choices 17592186052891] [:db/retract 17592186052887 :answer-field/choices 17592186052892] {:db/id 17592186054842 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6455f903-95ba-56a7-8ef0-339948a725c9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054371 :question/worked-solution "The number $7$ is multiplied by itself $6$ times, so we have

$$
5^{\color{blue}7} = \underbrace{5\cdot 5\cdot 5\cdot 5\cdot 5\cdot 5 \cdot 5}_{\large{\color{blue}7} \textrm{ copies of } 5}.
$$

The **exponent** $({\color{blue}7})$ says how many times the **base** $(5)$ is multiplied by itself.

Recall that $5^2$ is said as "five squared" and that $5^3$ is "five cubed." We don't have special names for larger exponents. However, we can say $5^7$  in several different ways:

- "five raised to the seventh power,"

- "five raised to the power seven,"

- "five to the seventh power,"

- "five to the power seven."

Raising to the power of one is special. Any number raised to the first power is itself. For example, $5^{\color{blue}1}$ means one copy of $5,$ so $5^{\color{blue}1} = 5.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054878 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186272018 :question/worked-solution "The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]$ such that $T(u)=v.$

This gives the following system of equations:

We express the cube root using the **radical symbol** $\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}.$

For example, the "cube root of $8$" equals $\color{blue}2$ since 

$$
{\color{blue}2}^3 = {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2} = 8.
$$

So, we write $\sqrt[3]{8}={\color{blue}2}.$

Some basic cube roots are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{0} & = & \sqrt[3]{{0}^{3}} & = & 0 \\ \sqrt[3]{1} & = & \sqrt[3]{{1}^{3}} & = & 1 \\ \sqrt[3]{8} & = & \sqrt[3]{{2}^{3}} & = & 2 \\ \sqrt[3]{27} & = & \sqrt[3]{{3}^{3}} & = & 3 \\ \sqrt[3]{64} & = & \sqrt[3]{{4}^{3}} & = & 4 \\ \sqrt[3]{125} & = & \sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}} & = & 5 \\ \sqrt[3]{1\,000} & = & \sqrt[3]{{10}^{3}} & = & 10\end{aligned}
$$

A **perfect cube** is a number whose cube root is a whole number. So, the numbers 

$$
0,\qquad 1,\qquad  8,\qquad  27,\qquad  64,\qquad 125, \qquad 1\,000
$$

 are all perfect cubes. You need to remember them." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121143 :tutorial/content "Unlike the square root, it *is* possible to find the cube root of a negative number.

For example, $\sqrt[3]{-8}={\color{blue}{-2}}$ because

$$
-8 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})^3 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}}).
$$

Some basic cube roots of negative numbers are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{-1} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-1)^{3}} & = & -1 \\ \sqrt[3]{-8} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-2)^{3}} & = & -2 \\ \sqrt[3]{-27} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-3)^{3}} & = & -3 \\ \sqrt[3]{-64} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-4)^{3}} & = & -4 \\ \sqrt[3]{-125} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-5)^{3}} & = & -5 \\ \sqrt[3]{-1\,000} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-10)^{3}} & = & -10\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the numbers 

$$
-1,\qquad  -8,\qquad  -27,\qquad  -64,\qquad -125, \qquad -1\,000
$$

are all perfect cubes." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121144 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate $(\sqrt[3]{64})^3$ by performing each operation one step at a time:

$$
\left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}64}\right)^3 = \left(\sqrt[3]{{\color{red}4}^3}\right)^3 = {\color{red}4}^3 = {\color{blue}64}
$$

Notice that cubing the cube root gives the number under the cube root:

$$
\left( \sqrt[3]{64} \right)^3 = 64
$$

This result holds in general. If $\color{blue}\square$ is any number, then

$$
\left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}\square}\right)^3 = {\color{blue}\square}.
$$

The cube and the cube root cancel each other out, and we're left with the number that we started with.

![](images/78/784f43f7253e1ed6fa394462a172e22571af06a5318b424ba2eab2157333c6fe.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121145 :tutorial/content "We can think of the cube root geometrically. For instance, let's represent the number $8$ by a collection of eight items:

![](images/36/3677ea5b5f875e12fdcc6376f6b29b43a663495d20a3fbf69b4937cc61661d79.png)

Now, we can pile them up in the form of a cube where each side is equal to $\sqrt[3]{8}={\color{blue}2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120026 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186127399 :answer-field/choices 17592186127400] [:db/retract 17592186127399 :answer-field/choices 17592186127401] [:db/retract 17592186127399 :answer-field/choices 17592186127402] [:db/retract 17592186127399 :answer-field/choices 17592186127403] [:db/retract 17592186127399 :answer-field/choices 17592186127404] {:db/id 17592186129191 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8" "question-00b86b57-002e-5667-8521-28c6ba4d5298" "question-2f7d21f4-2434-59d0-b158-63a98b31b96d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129190 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d9c15809-274b-5c74-bd5b-6fd325ecdfd9" "question-0e844cdc-bfeb-5b03-bf45-d36a53583297"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129189 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e49d891d-abb2-5ea6-ab4c-68e975346cd4" "question-cb97248a-192c-5cf9-ad2e-d068b8748779"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8" :question/id #uuid "8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-82209" :question/problem "Change the order of integration in the double integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2-{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/48/48a1ef0d61b8b81e2fa0649b95a329099d48a802a5339d730f2da9cf8b59f547.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le x\le 2-{y}^{2}\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=2-{y}^{2}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt{2-x},
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{2-x}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/22/22d41ecc443e1520035f52fefe524d88062432ab1643aa19b2e0b76185b191a0.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2-{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2-x}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0b369f9a-15dc-509e-a7b9-f81d6504e3a3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,2y-2\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=2y-2\,⟹\,y=\frac{x+2}{2},
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y=1.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le \frac{x+2}{2}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/54/543ffc57d0d32ae9a4bdefa87bd56deb7380061004b7737cf821117b4fb20e2f.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{2y-2}^{2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{(x+2)/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351403 :question/worked-solution "![](images/82/8287ba53b227ddc36aff486ea8d42a83203940ee265163320c19ad6cdb39089e.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$

"![](images/e6/e6b8889f9e8025cfca1ee0ae61b67a2f7ec9ec4aee15fab78d2f418a655bbcb8.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,{y}^{2}-1\le x\le 1-y\}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we need to split $D$ into two type I regions.

![](images/52/52640b30ded8bf2cd19fe7860c7640bde3c8427ae8978f32fb8020b2f7215468.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the left region, written in the form $y=y(x),$  are 

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=\sqrt{x+1}.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the right region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=1-x.$ 

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x+1}\}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-x\}.
$$

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{2}-1}^{1-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x+1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186388286 :question/worked-solution "![](images/9a/9a539f69187276895f8f53e2107c1959fefd0aeb7126dcff049569bfc8bc49d3.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type II regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y-2\le x\le 0\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y-2\le x\le 0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=y-2\,⟹\,y=x+2,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=-y-2\,⟹\,y=-x-2.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,-x-2\le y\le x+2\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/ba/ba9c9132c8efdb811e63bebc05e1f46bc8cbc54bcb8246072013a75d53bcb4df.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y-2}^{0}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y-2}^{0}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-x-2}^{x+2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351407 :question/worked-solution "![](images/0e/0e338b779e846bc3f5ac981c93f9cda65b63d654c1152aa423f855d12d7978d9.png)

{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le 1-{y}^{2}\}.
$$
