The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le \frac{1}{2}\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x)$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=\frac{x}{2}\,⟹\,x=2y.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le x\le 2y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/09/09f6f71eaf66fe10e73b80ae59a30ddd04478de71dbe37c749674ac9f10d5bd4.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x/2}^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})[{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})[x]_{0}^{2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}2y\,\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})]_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3e37bb84-408f-59ec-be8d-27de1ffdfa7d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3e37bb84-408f-59ec-be8d-27de1ffdfa7d" :answer-field/id #uuid "3e37bb84-408f-59ec-be8d-27de1ffdfa7d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-923eb37f-43b5-5b42-9f6f-7c5f6423cc9c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5b1155cd-f35f-5f58-8850-39c81d2ccf9e" "answer-923eb37f-43b5-5b42-9f6f-7c5f6423cc9c" "answer-7c39c2ee-43ff-5cba-b1e9-66bab554cd0a" "answer-8a2dc93b-07d2-5d02-9f1c-9af81857b7f7" "answer-a9e5f989-9f92-5708-89bc-01325d6b63d4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5b1155cd-f35f-5f58-8850-39c81d2ccf9e" :answer/id #uuid "5b1155cd-f35f-5f58-8850-39c81d2ccf9e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-923eb37f-43b5-5b42-9f6f-7c5f6423cc9c" :answer/id #uuid "923eb37f-43b5-5b42-9f6f-7c5f6423cc9c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{4})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7c39c2ee-43ff-5cba-b1e9-66bab554cd0a" :answer/id #uuid "7c39c2ee-43ff-5cba-b1e9-66bab554cd0a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8a2dc93b-07d2-5d02-9f1c-9af81857b7f7" :answer/id #uuid "8a2dc93b-07d2-5d02-9f1c-9af81857b7f7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a9e5f989-9f92-5708-89bc-01325d6b63d4" :answer/id #uuid "a9e5f989-9f92-5708-89bc-01325d6b63d4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{4})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186326683 :question/worked-solution "![](images/a8/a85f82756c621bf88b95451f54343be863345278f361fd0f0dd82f5d01c0cb5b.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le 1\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary is

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{y}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/82/8243a8c60e4b8b4846d330a00a090d6f93f94f17323c1d0a88d486ba77745451.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{y}}\frac{3{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{y}}\frac{3{x}^{5}}{\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{[\frac{2}{6}\sqrt{{x}^{6}+{y}^{2}}]}_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{2{y}^{2}}-\sqrt{{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{2}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{(\sqrt{2}-1)}{2}[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129653 :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{3}+\pi )\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/19/19d2d5698ad6b22c003b44d1a023c56ae7779a6d26345732bace3723062f6e0d.png)

$$

$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$

$$

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{3}+\pi )\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{3}+\pi )\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{3}+\pi )[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{3}+\pi )[x]_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{3}+\pi )\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{3}+\pi )}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8+\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(8+\pi )}{3}.\end{aligned}

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 4-{x}^{2}\}.

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$

$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{4-y}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-y}\},

![](images/48/48c874b069b55599f76a8fe1aa50c5f4db36ff8943d264a107452668d689174b.png)

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186381020 :question/worked-solution "First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{x}^{2}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{6}-0)dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{5}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{5}\,dy & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{32}{3}-\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{21}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186382490 :question/problem "Calculate ${∬}_{D}y{e}^{x}\,dA,$ where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,{y}^{2}\le x\le 2-{y}^{2}\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,{y}^{2}\le x\le 2-{y}^{2}\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y{e}^{x}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{2-{y}^{2}}(y\cdot {e}^{x})\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{2-{y}^{2}}(y\cdot {e}^{x})\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{2-{y}^{2}}{e}^{x}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{e}^{x}]_{{y}^{2}}^{2-{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y({e}^{2-{y}^{2}}-{e}^{{y}^{2}})dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y{e}^{2-{y}^{2}}-y{e}^{{y}^{2}})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y{e}^{2-{y}^{2}}-y{e}^{{y}^{2}})\,dy & ={[-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2-{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{y}^{2}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}({e}^{1}+{e}^{1}-({e}^{2}+{e}^{0})) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-2e+1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186407922 :question/worked-solution "Notice that $D$ is a type II region. Since $x\ge 0,$ we obtain the following equations in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4 & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}} \\ y=2-x & \,⟹\,x=2-y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}} & =2-y \\ 4-{y}^{2} & =(2-y)^{2} \\ 4-{y}^{2} & =4-4y+{y}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{2}-4y & =0 \\ y(y-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=1,$ the $y$-limits are 
$1\le y\le 2.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](images/f8/f8fedf15e26f64fc344bd7db6ffaa659bd7c130f36f4a39389b6108136836104.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,2-y\le x\le \sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}\}.

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}x\,dA={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{2-y}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\,x\,dx\,dy
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{2-y}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\,x\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{2-y}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}x\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\,\frac{1}{2}[\,{x}^{2}\,]_{2-y}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\,\frac{1}{2}(4-{y}^{2}-(2-y)^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\,(2y-{y}^{2})dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,(2y-{y}^{2})dy & ={[{y}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(4-\frac{8}{3})-(1-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a9c36b7d-47cc-5c7c-bf98-1c203381319d" :question/id #uuid "a9c36b7d-47cc-5c7c-bf98-1c203381319d" :question/math-academy-id "q-132532" :question/problem "Calculate ${∬}_{D}2y{e}^{x}\,dA,$ where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}\}.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}} & =\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}} \\ 1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =4-{y}^{2} \\ 4-{y}^{2} & =16-4{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{2} & =12 \\ {y}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\sqrt{1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}}\le x\le \sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}\}.

$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134021 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064221 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bf661221-c0cb-55d5-9d95-0e82e6a1207a" "question-3a566b97-b1a6-51f5-a466-0f0acaf448eb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064082 :question/problem "What is $9^0?$" :question/worked-solution "Any number raised to the power of zero is equal to $1.$ So,

$$
2^0 = 1 \quad\textrm{and}\quad (-55)^0=1.
$$

To understand why, let's try to convince ourselves that $2^0 = 1.$ First, we write down a table containing all of the powers of $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{4} & =16 \\ {2}^{3} & =8 \\ {2}^{2} & =4 \\ {2}^{1} & =2 \\ {2}^{0} & =◻\,?\end{aligned}
$$

As we go down the list, the number in blue is divided by $2$ each time. Following this pattern, we must have 

$$
2^{\color{red}{0}}  = {\color{blue}{2}}\div 2 = 1.
$$

It doesn't matter whether the number is positive or negative, a fraction or a decimal, big or small. Raising any non-zero number to the power of zero always gives $1.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064414 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186268857 :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region.

![](images/01/019f0f9f83ddf323d543d109677335cb3ae72a200baf834453a0eca16a9353ba.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/d2/d222e86f6af7c3ed2b35711114c9062d6f0c9b0f2551aa44cac33318c6e5813f.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,x+2\le y\le \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\le y\le x+2\}.

$$"] [17592186130400 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the double integral  

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 2(x+y)\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the finite region bounded by the lines $x=0, \, y=1, \, y=2, \, y=3-x,$ and $y=x.$ How do we proceed?

To evaluate an integral like this, we carry out the following steps: 

**Step 1.** Sketch the region $D$. This allows us to determine the precise set-up of our integral. 

In this example, we obtain the following:

![](images/0a/0a90a4f377327f5293308f1e08ac6596f1c27b9bd47a614d6d7cb1c5dbfec33c.png)

**Step 2.** Split (if necessary) the region $D$ into several type I or II regions.

From the diagram above, we see that our region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as follows.

![](images/a9/a93e1a0a0a7f9c104cb5d380b2a7ff98d6712ef0d2d67b74130da5dcf1701443.png)

 

So, we get

$$
D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq 1, \quad 1 \leq y \leq 2\big\}
$$

and

$$
D_2= \{(x,y)\: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 3/2,  \quad  x \leq y \leq 3-x\}
$$

**Step 3.** Set up and evaluate the integral using the additivity property of double integrals. We recall the following fact:

*If $D$ is the union of two sub-regions, $D_1, D_2$, that don't overlap then,*

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A.
$$

So, finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}2(x+y)\text{ }dy\,dx+{\int }_{1}^{3/2}{\int }_{x}^{3-x}2(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186129341 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0] [17592186054349 :question/worked-solution "The polynomial $1+2x^2 - 8x$ has three terms, so it is a trinomial.

["question-2c70515f-461b-5406-a00b-651a86f2659d" :question/math-academy-id "q-152252"] ["question-2c70515f-461b-5406-a00b-651a86f2659d" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $5{x}^{2}-7x+1$ is cubic trinomial.

- Statement I is false. Since the degree of the trinomial $5{x}^{2}-7x+1$ is $2,$ it is a quadratic trinomial.

- Statement II is true. Since the degree of the trinomial ${x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+x$ is $3,$ it is a cubic trinomial.

- Statement III is true. A trinomial *could be* cubic (see, for example, statement II). 

 However, a trinomial is *not always* cubic (see, for example, statement I). 

 So, some trinomials are cubic.

["question-298a3ab5-9f3b-5907-82bb-2239de27222c" :question/math-academy-id "q-152438"] ["question-298a3ab5-9f3b-5907-82bb-2239de27222c" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The product of $7x$ and $3{x}^{2}$ is a binomial.

II. The product of $4x$ and $5$ is a monomial.

III. The product of two monomials is **always** a binomial."] ["question-298a3ab5-9f3b-5907-82bb-2239de27222c" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
(7x)\times (3{x}^{2})=21{x}^{3},
$$

which is *not* a binomial (it's a monomial).

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
(4x)\times (5)=20x,
$$

which is a monomial.

- Statement III is false. There are products of two monomials that are not binomials (see, for example, statement I and II).

In fact, the product of two monomials is *never* a binomial.

"question-298a3ab5-9f3b-5907-82bb-2239de27222c"] [17592186055997 :tutorial/content "Polynomials with one, two, or three terms have special names.

- A polynomial with one term is called a **monomial**. For example:
 

$$
1, \qquad y,	\qquad	2x^3,	\qquad	5a^{4}
$$

However, the following expressions are not monomials because they can't be called polynomials:
 

$$
\dfrac{1}{y},	\qquad	5t^{-1},	\qquad \sqrt{x}, \qquad 	2z^{1/4}
$$

- A polynomial with two terms is called a **binomial**. For example:

$$
x+3,	\qquad	7n^2 +n,	\qquad	p^{32} -1
$$

- A polynomial with three terms is called a **trinomial**. For example:
 

$$
z^2 -z +1,	\qquad	x^3 -2x -1,	\qquad	2c^{4} - 3c^{3} +4c^2
$$"] [17592186055998 :tutorial/content "Each type of polynomial of degree between $0$ and $5$ has a specific name. These are shown in the table below.

| Degree | Name | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | Constant | $7$ |
| $1$ | Linear | $3x + 2$ |
| $2$ | Quadratic | $2x^2 - 6x + 1$ |
| $3$ | Cubic | $x^3 + 4x^2 + 9x$ |
| $4$ | Quartic | $3x^4 - 5x^2$ |
| $5$ | Quintic | $7x^5 + 3x^4 - x^4 + x - 6$ |

We can combine these with the names we learned earlier. 

For example:

- $2x+1$ is a *linear binomial* because its degree equals $1,$ and it has $2$ terms.

- $x^2$ is a *quadratic monomial* because its degree equals $2,$ and it has $1$ term.

- $2x^3+x+1$ is a *cubic trinomial* because its degree equals $3,$ and it has $3$ terms.

If a polynomial contains more than three terms, then we refer to it by its degree only.

For example:

- $x^3+2x^2+x-1$ is a *cubic polynomial.*

- $x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1$ is a *quartic polynomial.*"] [17592186054924 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/id #uuid "fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff"] ["question-fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-162559"] ["question-fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/problem "![](images/80/804976bf326ed561ff8e7b4f5a6c65361039a686a4449edfdf8e6f497ee5cbda.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$"] ["question-fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/de/de9eb8381df05d2d5e6222a51b0ccbc5729e522df94a4aace570881d1226a1ca.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xz]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}-z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}z-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[x]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =(-1)+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2652e0ca-544c-51d5-827f-9347b3d96ac0" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 \\ 20 & 8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8+4\text{i} & -4 \\ 20 & 8+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-8+4\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 20{x}_{1}+(8+4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=4\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$"] ["question-b50cc60c-3830-586d-ac40-7d3e6216a024" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ba768c88-4eb0-5381-9499-0a94fd8cffce" :answer-field/id #uuid "ba768c88-4eb0-5381-9499-0a94fd8cffce"] ["answer-4ee66ee4-6517-5668-9169-22b519673baf" :answer/id #uuid "4ee66ee4-6517-5668-9169-22b519673baf"] ["answer-4ee66ee4-6517-5668-9169-22b519673baf" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4ee66ee4-6517-5668-9169-22b519673baf" :answer/value "-4.096"] ["answer-field-ba768c88-4eb0-5381-9499-0a94fd8cffce" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-ba768c88-4eb0-5381-9499-0a94fd8cffce" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-ba768c88-4eb0-5381-9499-0a94fd8cffce" :answer-field/correct "answer-4ee66ee4-6517-5668-9169-22b519673baf"] ["answer-field-ba768c88-4eb0-5381-9499-0a94fd8cffce" :answer-field/choices "answer-4ee66ee4-6517-5668-9169-22b519673baf"] ["question-b50cc60c-3830-586d-ac40-7d3e6216a024" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-ba768c88-4eb0-5381-9499-0a94fd8cffce"] [17592186133741 :knowledge-point/questions "question-b50cc60c-3830-586d-ac40-7d3e6216a024"] [17592186135183 :tutorial/content "To **cube** a number means to multiply that number by itself and then multiply the result by the original number once more.

For example, to "cube $2$", we need to multiply $2$ by $2$ to make $4,$ and then multiply this result by $2$ once more. We write the "cube of $2$" as $2^3,$ so we have

$$
2^3 = \underbrace{2\cdot 2}_{\large 4} \cdot 2 = 4 \cdot 2 = 8.
$$

We would then say that "the cube of $2$ is $8$". We could also say "$2$ cubed equals $8$".

The number ${\color{blue}3}$ in the expression $2^{\color{blue}3}$ is called the power (or exponent).

The act of cubing a number can be represented geometrically. For example, let's start by representing the number $2$ with the following collection of two items:

![](images/b6/b6a13017dcbcf25a66ab576189690e8879a4ccbb3c4c5562b129f4dd15af4e85.png)

Then we can picture $2^3$ by creating a bigger shape (called a **cube**) with length, width and height all equal to $2\mathbin{:}$

![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png)

There are $8$ items in total in our big cube (one little cube is hiding behind the others), indicating that $2^3=8.$

Clearly, $1^3=1\cdot1\cdot1={\color{blue}1}.$ The next few first basic cubes are shown below:

| $2^3=2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2={\color{blue}8}$ | $3^3=3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3={\color{blue}27}$ | $4^3=4 \cdot 4 \cdot 4={\color{blue}64}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png) | ![](images/cb/cb3171dc7f7a2e9838c3e8b46c3ce385be28624b4474391b9bb211b5a599fa55.png) | ![](images/65/6546ffc5df407b29df601252e1f5afa8e01b17dca5c7169a6321d550d86255c3.png) |

The cubes of our usual counting numbers are called **cube numbers** or **perfect cubes**. We can write them as follows:

$$
1^3, 2^3, 3^3, 4^3, 5^3, 6^3, \ldots \qquad \text{or} \qquad {\color{blue}1}, {\color{blue}8}, {\color{blue}27}, {\color{blue}64}, {\color{blue}125}, {\color{blue}216}, \ldots
$$"] [17592186135184 :tutorial/content "Cubing a negative number *always* results in another negative number.

This is because a negative times a negative gives a positive value, and then a positive times a negative is a negative again:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,{{(-)\,\cdot \,(-)}_{⏟}}_{(+)}\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(+)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(-)\end{aligned}
$$

For example,

$$
({\color{red}-5})^3 = \underbrace{({\color{red}-5}) \cdot ({\color{red}-5})}_{\large {\color{blue}25}} \cdot ({\color{red}-5}) = {\color{blue}25} \cdot ({\color{red}-5}) = {\color{red}-125}.
$$"] [17592186134039 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" :question/id #uuid "ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945"] ["question-ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" :question/math-academy-id "q-140315"] ["question-ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$"] ["question-ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -3-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 8 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-8) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -5)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -20) & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)(\lambda +4)(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda -5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=5$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-4}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-4})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=5.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{5}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-5I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 5\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -8 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+8{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5.$ So,

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{5})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-4})+\text{dim}({V}_{5})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, a corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-ed2c40c3-1b90-504b-a86e-ac9274a7e945" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-e4a53fb3-00cc-58aa-aebb-3f7e25363f55" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 4 & -7 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -1 \\ 4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )+4) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25) & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -5)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=5$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=2.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{2}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{2})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=5.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{5}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-5I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & -7 & 3\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & -7 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). This implies that we will have $3-2=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{5})=1.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is *not* diagonalizable, since 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{2})+\text{dim}({V}_{5})=1+1=2\ne 3.\,\times 
$$"] ["question-e9c15a3d-862e-553a-bd17-8b80866daf10" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7b9e7048-3689-53e4-bb31-2f73b280aea1" :answer-field/id #uuid Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=7.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{7}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{7})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{4}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-4I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 7\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{4})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{7})+\text{dim}({V}_{4})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, the corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-63615617-5b80-58c9-8714-0059cfaa1f62" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-9e1fd6c2-27d9-583f-935b-d3e4748c1c08" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-6.$ So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-6})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{12})+\text{dim}({V}_{-6})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

$$

$$

[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]

$$"] ["question-e4fbd5e6-b819-591a-880c-a933bdaba9d3" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨2,0,2⟩\times ⟨1,4,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-8i+2j+8k \\  & =⟨-8,2,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =⟨-15,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨2,3,1⟩+w⟨-3,-2,3⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130 \\ ⟨2-3w,3-2w,1+3w⟩\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130 \\ -8(2-3w)+2(3-2w)+8(1+3w) & =130 \\ -16+24w+6-4w+8+24w & =130 \\ 44w & =132 \\ w & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=3$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨2-3(3),3-2(3),1+3(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-7,-3,10⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨5,3,-7⟩+t⟨4,-3,2⟩,\,Π:5x+2y-7z-15=0.
$$"] ["question-42cfce4b-bf3d-5d7e-8fad-15e0c813875c" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨5+4t,3-3t,-7+2t⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2y-7z-15 & =0 \\ 5x+2y-7z & =15 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨5,2,-7⟩ & =15 \\ r\cdot ⟨5,2,-7⟩ & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨5+4t,3-3t,-7+2t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨5,2,-7⟩ & =15 \\ ⟨5+4t,3-3t,-7+2t⟩\cdot ⟨5,2,-7⟩ & =15 \\ 5(5+4t)+2(3-3t)-7(-7+2t) & =15 \\ 25+20t+6-6t+49-14t & =15 \\ 80 & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has no solution. Therefore, we conclude that the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ do not intersect."] ["question-42cfce4b-bf3d-5d7e-8fad-15e0c813875c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$"] [17592186188088 :question/problem "Simplify the expression $-9v-4(3+5v).$"] [17592186188088 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the expression we need to subtract from $-9v$ must be expanded using the distributive law. 

So first, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
-9v - \Big[4(3+5v)\Big]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
-9v - \Big[12+20v\Big].
$$

Now, we remove the brackets by distributing the negative sign. This gives

$$
-9v - 12 - 20v.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9v-12-20v & = \\ (-9v-20v)-12 & = \\ -29v-12 & \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186188089 :question/problem "Simplify the expression $10 - 2(3x - 4).$"] [17592186188089 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the expression we need to subtract from $10$ must be expanded using the distributive law. 

So first, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
10 - \Big[2(3x-4)\Big]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
10 - \Big[6x-8\Big].
$$

Now, we remove the brackets by distributing the negative sign. This gives

$$
10 - 6x + 8.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}10-6x+8 & = \\ (10+8)-6x & = \\ 18-6x & \end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f10306d0-b077-5314-9baa-700a263e9595" :question/id #uuid "f10306d0-b077-5314-9baa-700a263e9595"] ["question-f10306d0-b077-5314-9baa-700a263e9595" :question/math-academy-id "q-171523"] ["question-f10306d0-b077-5314-9baa-700a263e9595" :question/problem "The expression $-a-(3a+1)$ can be written as{{field-1}}

So first, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
15-[3(k+3)]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
15-[3k+9].
$$

Now, we remove the brackets by distributing the negative sign. This gives

$$
15-3k-9.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}15-3k-9 & = \\ (15-9)-3k & = \\ 6-3\,k & \end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8e87c3a3-adbf-5bc1-93e9-45cedd31d826" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d16d18e8-ecbb-53f2-b58f-64ff0cd149b7" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-effd2690-1ce3-5bfd-837f-fb52a891061c" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the expression we need to subtract from $7$ must be expanded using the distributive law.

$$
7-[2(4b-3)]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
7-[8b-6].
$$

Now, we remove the brackets by distributing the negative sign. This gives

$$
7-8b+6.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}7-8b+6 & = \\ (7+6)-8b & = \\ 13-8b & \end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-effd2690-1ce3-5bfd-837f-fb52a891061c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-3e868b29-0793-5cd6-9a3d-fe9a4f09f0db" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-effd2690-1ce3-5bfd-837f-fb52a891061c"] [17592186189440 :tutorial/content "Let's think about how to simplify the following expression:

$$
6x-(3+2x)
$$

In this example, we're subtracting the entire group of terms in parentheses from $6x.$ In such cases, we distribute the negative sign to each term in the parentheses *first* and then simplify by collecting like terms.

Removing the parentheses by distributing the negative sign, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-(3+2x) & = \\ 6x-3-2x & .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-3-2x & = \\ (6x-2x)-3 & = \\ 4x-3 & \end{aligned}
$$

Let's take a look at another example."] [17592186189441 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, to subtract a group of terms, we have to apply the distributive law.

For example, let's simplify the following expression:

$$
7-4(y+2)
$$

First, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
7 - \Big[4(y+2)\Big]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
7 - \Big[4y+8\Big].
$$

Now, we proceed as before. Removing the brackets by distributing the negative sign gives

$$
7 - 4y - 8.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}7-4y-8 & = \\ (7-8)-4y & = \\ -1-4y & \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186188467 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/id #uuid "83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb"] ["question-83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/math-academy-id "q-129409"] ["question-83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist"] ["question-83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$"] ["question-83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-cbe5df83-a1f1-5212-94d6-8a03a2936996" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z)\text{ }k \\  & =(1-2xz)\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j-{x}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(\,1-2(1)(2)\,)\text{ }i+2(1)\text{ }j-(1)^{2}k \\  & =-3\,i+2\,j-1\,k \\  & =⟨-3,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-3,2,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d960c3a0-bbd5-5487-b90e-ade524992bee" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b758f2b0-ee02-5c9d-8c7b-99e5dc8caa68" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-58a67d8c-4e10-594d-863e-d6da9c98fcce" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}z+{z}^{2}y+{y}^{2}x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}z+{z}^{2}y+{y}^{2}x)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}z+{z}^{2}y+{y}^{2}x)\text{ }k \\  & =(2xz+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({z}^{2}+2yx)\text{ }j+({x}^{2}+2zy)k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,-1) & =(2(1)(-1)+{1}^{2})\text{ }i+((-1)^{2}+2(1)(1))\text{ }j+({1}^{2}+2(-1)(1))k \\  & =-\,i+3\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,3,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-1,3,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ -(x-1)+3(y-1)-(z+1) & =0 \\ -x+3y-z-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-58a67d8c-4e10-594d-863e-d6da9c98fcce" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bd5c8610-318e-58b9-8590-725b9e0fa2c5" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-417fb447-d242-53ba-be44-8afd73288884" :question/worked-solution "Let's define  $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+{e}^{z-1}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=17.$

["question-2dcb9c2a-7362-5965-b423-4b434eec8d3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-102714"] ["question-2dcb9c2a-7362-5965-b423-4b434eec8d3a" :question/problem "Consider the surface $x{y}^{2}+6=z{x}^{2}.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(-2,-1,1).$"] ["question-2dcb9c2a-7362-5965-b423-4b434eec8d3a" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2}+6 & =z{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2} & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(-2,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}-z{x}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =({y}^{2}-2xz)\text{ }i+2xy\text{ }j-{x}^{2}\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(-2,-1,1) & =((-1)^{2}-2(-2)(1))\text{ }i+2(-2)(-1)\text{ }j-(-2)^{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5\,i+4j-4\,k \\  & =⟨5,4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(-2,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+1,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨5,4,-4⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+1,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ 5(x+2)+4(y+1)-4(z-1) & =0 \\ 5x+4y-4z+18 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2dcb9c2a-7362-5965-b423-4b434eec8d3a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f5f7cc0c-f2cb-5ebd-8a19-e3ddc8cdda4a" :answer-field/id #uuid }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2),$ what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$"] ["question-480ef21f-535f-5e73-9903-6cc50742dda8" :question/worked-solution "Let's define  $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=2+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)k \\  & =(-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-yz)i+(-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-xz)j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xy)k \\ ∇f(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2) & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{ }i+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-2(\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{ }j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\frac{\pi }{2})(-\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{ }k \\  & =\pi \text{ }i-\pi \text{ }j+(1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4})\text{ }k \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,-\pi ,\,1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨\pi ,\,-\pi ,\,\frac{{\pi }^{2}+4}{4}⟩.$

will learn how to compute the tangent plane to the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k,$ where $k$ is a constant, at some point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0).$ 

As an example, consider the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2 +y^2+z.
$$

 

Suppose that we wish to find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=  (1,1, 2).$ 

Evaluating $f$ at the point $(1,1,2),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = (1)^2 +(1)^2+2 = 4.
$$

 

So, the equation of our level surface is

$$
x^2 +y^2+z = 4.
$$

Now, to find the equation of the tangent plane to this surface at $(1,1,2),$ we can use the following result:

  *Given a hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ and a point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0,y_0,z_0)$ that lies in the domain of $f$, the gradient $\nabla \! f (\mathbf x_0)$ is normal to the tangent plane of the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k$ at the point $\mathbf x_0$*. 

![](images/11/1140e80fbb2efd684311cb7625e5b0be361d6fb951036253f57b9e51234de3ee.png)

       

We can now find the equation of the tangent plane to our level surface.

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $\mathbf x_0 = (1,1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}\,i+{f}_{y}\,j+{f}_{z}\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(1,1,2) & =2(1)\text{ }i+2(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =2\text{ }i+2\text{ }j+k \\  & =⟨2,\,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally,  we write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\nabla f(1,1,2) \cdot \langle x-1, \: y-1, \: z-2 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\langle 2,\:2,\:1\rangle\cdot \langle x-1, y-1, z-2\rangle &= 0\[3pt]
      2(x-1)+ 2(y-1) + (z-2) & =0\
      2x +2y +z -6&=0   
}
$$"] [17592186129332 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0] [17592186054371 :question/worked-solution "The number $7$ is multiplied by itself $6$ times, so we have

The **exponent** $({\color{blue}7})$ says how many times the **base** $(5)$ is multiplied by itself.

Recall that $5^2$ is said as "five squared" and that $5^3$ is "five cubed." We don't have special names for larger exponents. However, we can say $5^7$  in several different ways:

- "five raised to the seventh power,"

- "five raised to the power seven,"

- "five to the seventh power,"

- "five to the power seven."

"question-48d4be4c-58b6-582c-9132-4582bd4667fc"] [17592186121142 :tutorial/content "Finding the **cube root** of a number is the reverse of cubing a number. We express the cube root using the **radical symbol** $\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}.$

For example, the "cube root of $8$" equals $\color{blue}2$ since 

$$
{\color{blue}2}^3 = {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2} = 8.
$$

So, we write $\sqrt[3]{8}={\color{blue}2}.$

Some basic cube roots are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{0} & = & \sqrt[3]{{0}^{3}} & = & 0 \\ \sqrt[3]{1} & = & \sqrt[3]{{1}^{3}} & = & 1 \\ \sqrt[3]{8} & = & \sqrt[3]{{2}^{3}} & = & 2 \\ \sqrt[3]{27} & = & \sqrt[3]{{3}^{3}} & = & 3 \\ \sqrt[3]{64} & = & \sqrt[3]{{4}^{3}} & = & 4 \\ \sqrt[3]{125} & = & \sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}} & = & 5 \\ \sqrt[3]{1\,000} & = & \sqrt[3]{{10}^{3}} & = & 10\end{aligned}
$$

A **perfect cube** is a number whose cube root is a whole number. So, the numbers 

$$
0,\qquad 1,\qquad  8,\qquad  27,\qquad  64,\qquad 125, \qquad 1\,000
$$

 are all perfect cubes. You need to remember them."] [17592186121143 :tutorial/content "Unlike the square root, it *is* possible to find the cube root of a negative number.

For example, $\sqrt[3]{-8}={\color{blue}{-2}}$ because

$$
-8 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})^3 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}}).
$$

Some basic cube roots of negative numbers are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{-1} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-1)^{3}} & = & -1 \\ \sqrt[3]{-8} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-2)^{3}} & = & -2 \\ \sqrt[3]{-27} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-3)^{3}} & = & -3 \\ \sqrt[3]{-64} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-4)^{3}} & = & -4 \\ \sqrt[3]{-125} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-5)^{3}} & = & -5 \\ \sqrt[3]{-1\,000} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-10)^{3}} & = & -10\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the numbers 

$$
-1,\qquad  -8,\qquad  -27,\qquad  -64,\qquad -125, \qquad -1\,000
$$

are all perfect cubes."] [17592186121144 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate $(\sqrt[3]{64})^3$ by performing each operation one step at a time:

$$
\left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}64}\right)^3 = \left(\sqrt[3]{{\color{red}4}^3}\right)^3 = {\color{red}4}^3 = {\color{blue}64}
$$

Notice that cubing the cube root gives the number under the cube root:

$$
\left( \sqrt[3]{64} \right)^3 = 64
$$

This result holds in general. If $\color{blue}\square$ is any number, then

$$
\left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}\square}\right)^3 = {\color{blue}\square}.
$$

The cube and the cube root cancel each other out, and we're left with the number that we started with.

![](images/78/784f43f7253e1ed6fa394462a172e22571af06a5318b424ba2eab2157333c6fe.png)"] [17592186121145 :tutorial/content "We can think of the cube root geometrically. For instance, let's represent the number $8$ by a collection of eight items:

![](images/36/3677ea5b5f875e12fdcc6376f6b29b43a663495d20a3fbf69b4937cc61661d79.png)

Now, we can pile them up in the form of a cube where each side is equal to $\sqrt[3]{8}={\color{blue}2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png)"] [17592186120026 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8" :question/id #uuid "8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8"] ["question-8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-82209"] ["question-8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8" :question/problem "Change the order of integration in the double integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2-{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$"] ["question-8d54021f-0d37-540b-875f-4f433fa4e2b8" :question/worked-solution "![](images/48/48a1ef0d61b8b81e2fa0649b95a329099d48a802a5339d730f2da9cf8b59f547.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le x\le 2-{y}^{2}\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=2-{y}^{2}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt{2-x},
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,{y}^{2}-1\le x\le 1-y\}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we need to split $D$ into two type I regions.

![](images/52/52640b30ded8bf2cd19fe7860c7640bde3c8427ae8978f32fb8020b2f7215468.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the left region, written in the form $y=y(x),$  are 

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=\sqrt{x+1}.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the right region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=1-x.$ 

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x+1}\}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-x\}.
$$

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{2}-1}^{1-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x+1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186388286 :question/worked-solution "![](images/9a/9a539f69187276895f8f53e2107c1959fefd0aeb7126dcff049569bfc8bc49d3.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type II regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y-2\le x\le 0\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y-2\le x\le 0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=y-2\,⟹\,y=x+2,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=-y-2\,⟹\,y=-x-2.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,-x-2\le y\le x+2\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/ba/ba9c9132c8efdb811e63bebc05e1f46bc8cbc54bcb8246072013a75d53bcb4df.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y-2}^{0}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y-2}^{0}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-x-2}^{x+2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186351407 :question/worked-solution "![](images/0e/0e338b779e846bc3f5ac981c93f9cda65b63d654c1152aa423f855d12d7978d9.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le \sqrt{1-x}\}.

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le \frac{1}{2}\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x)$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=\frac{x}{2}\,⟹\,x=2y.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le x\le 2y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/09/09f6f71eaf66fe10e73b80ae59a30ddd04478de71dbe37c749674ac9f10d5bd4.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x/2}^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})[{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})[x]_{0}^{2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}2y\,\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})]_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e49d891d-abb2-5ea6-ab4c-68e975346cd4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-3e37bb84-408f-59ec-be8d-27de1ffdfa7d" :answer-field/id #uuid The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le 1\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary is

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{y}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/82/8243a8c60e4b8b4846d330a00a090d6f93f94f17323c1d0a88d486ba77745451.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

["question-cb97248a-192c-5cf9-ad2e-d068b8748779" :question/worked-solution "![](images/7e/7e0a0b1860f316f7954e85b9d7f6567d9e0c05bf316cb8af3901037abe6fd17e.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡5,\,{e}^{y}\le x\le 5\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x={e}^{y}\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 5,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/3c/3c95dd90ad02ab708f5893e47e7d7d0c8a212c18aed1972fb1bba1362181c383.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{\int }_{{e}^{y}}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{5}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x)[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x)\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x)\,{|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡5-5)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\operatorname{ln}⁡1-1) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡5-5).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-cb97248a-192c-5cf9-ad2e-d068b8748779" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-37f743ed-c677-5ee3-8526-cdbc90d5f567" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
2^0 = 1 \quad\textrm{and}\quad (-55)^0=1.
$$

To understand why, let's try to convince ourselves that $2^0 = 1.$ First, we write down a table containing all of the powers of $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{4} & =16 \\ {2}^{3} & =8 \\ {2}^{2} & =4 \\ {2}^{1} & =2 \\ {2}^{0} & =◻\,?\end{aligned}
$$

As we go down the list, the number in blue is divided by $2$ each time. Following this pattern, we must have 

$$
2^{\color{red}{0}}  = {\color{blue}{2}}\div 2 = 1.
$$

It doesn't matter whether the number is positive or negative, a fraction or a decimal, big or small. $$"] [17592186130400 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the double integral  

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 2(x+y)\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the finite region bounded by the lines $x=0, \, y=1, \, y=2, \, y=3-x,$ and $y=x.$ How do we proceed?

To evaluate an integral like this, we carry out the following steps: 

**Step 1.** Sketch the region $D$. This allows us to determine the precise set-up of our integral. 

In this example, we obtain the following:

![](images/0a/0a90a4f377327f5293308f1e08ac6596f1c27b9bd47a614d6d7cb1c5dbfec33c.png)

**Step 2.** Split (if necessary) the region $D$ into several type I or II regions.

From the diagram above, we see that our region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as follows.

![](images/a9/a93e1a0a0a7f9c104cb5d380b2a7ff98d6712ef0d2d67b74130da5dcf1701443.png)

So, we get

$$
D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq 1, \quad 1 \leq y \leq 2\big\}
$$

and

$$
D_2= \{(x,y)\: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 3/2,  \quad  x \leq y \leq 3-x\}
$$

**Step 3.** Set up and evaluate the integral using the additivity property of double integrals. We recall the following fact:

> *If $D$ is the union of two sub-regions, $D_1, D_2$, that don't overlap then,*
> 
> 
> $$
> \iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A.
> $$

So, finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}2(x+y)\text{ }dy\,dx+{\int }_{1}^{3/2}{\int }_{x}^{3-x}2(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186054349 :question/worked-solution "The polynomial $1+2x^2 - 8x$ has three terms, so it is a trinomial.

Also, its degree is $2$, so it is quadratic.

Therefore, the polynomial is a quadratic trinomial."] [17592186054350 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

For example, to "cube $2$", we need to multiply $2$ by $2$ to make $4$, and then multiply this result by $2$ once more. We write the "cube of $2$" as $2^3$, so we have

$$
2^3 = \underbrace{2\cdot 2}_{\large 4} \cdot 2 = 4 \cdot 2 = 8
$$

We would then say that "the cube of $2$ is $8$". We could also say "$2$ cubed equals $8$".

The number ${\color{blue}3}$ in the expression $2^{\color{blue}3}$ is called the power (or exponent).

The act of cubing a number can be represented geometrically. For example, let's start by representing the number $2$ with the following collection of two items:

![](images/b6/b6a13017dcbcf25a66ab576189690e8879a4ccbb3c4c5562b129f4dd15af4e85.png)

Then we can picture $2^3$ by creating a bigger shape (called a **cube**) with length, width and height all equal to $2$:

![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png)

There are $8$ items in total in our big cube (one little cube is hiding behind the others), indicating that $2^3=8$.

Clearly,

$$
1^3=1\cdot1\cdot1={\color{blue}1}
$$

The next few first basic cubes are shown below:

| $2^3=2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2={\color{blue}8}$ | $3^3=3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3={\color{blue}27}$ | $4^3=4 \cdot 4 \cdot 4={\color{blue}64}$ |

| ![](images/30/305e02bdaa4c3efcb9d8047eeb3d3573f39c08714e30ba6053cfc4441053156b.png) | ![](images/cb/cb3171dc7f7a2e9838c3e8b46c3ce385be28624b4474391b9bb211b5a599fa55.png) | ![](images/65/6546ffc5df407b29df601252e1f5afa8e01b17dca5c7169a6321d550d86255c3.png) |

$1^3, 2^3, 3^3, 4^3, 5^3, 6^3, \ldots \qquad \text{or} \qquad {\color{blue}1}, {\color{blue}8}, {\color{blue}27}, {\color{blue}64}, {\color{blue}125}, {\color{blue}216}, \ldots$"] [17592186135184 :tutorial/content "Cubing a negative number *always* results in another negative number.

$$"] [17592186130327 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to compute the tangent plane to the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k,$ where $k$ is a constant, at some point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0).$ 

As an example, consider the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2 +y^2+z.
$$

 

Suppose that we wish to find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=  (1,1, 2).$ 

Evaluating $f$ at the point $(1,1,2),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = (1)^2 +(1)^2+2 = 4.
$$

 

So, the equation of our level surface is

$$
x^2 +y^2+z = 4.
$$

Now, to find the equation of the tangent plane to this surface at $(1,1,2),$ we can use the following result:

> *Given a hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ and a point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0,y_0,z_0)$ that lies in the domain of $f$, the gradient $\nabla \! f (\mathbf x_0)$ is normal to the tangent plane of the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k$ at the point $\mathbf x_0$*.

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186064611 :question/problem "Calculate the value of $(\frac{9}{8})^{0}$."] [17592186065360 :tutorial/content "Any number raised to the power of zero is equal to $1$. For example,

$$
2^0 = 1 \quad\textrm{and}\quad (-55)^0=1
$$

To understand why, let's try to convince ourselves that $2^0 = 1$. First, we write down a table containing all of the powers of $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2^{4} &= 16 \\
2^{3} &= 8 \\
2^{2} &= 4 \\
2^{1} &= 2 \\
2^{0} &= ◻
\end{aligned}
$$

As we go down the list, the number in blue is divided by $2$ each time. Following this pattern, we must have

$$
2^{\color{red}{0}} = {\color{blue}{2}}\div 2 = 1
$$

It doesn't matter whether the number is positive or negative, a fraction or a decimal, big or small. Raising any non-zero number to the power of zero always gives $1$."]]}

Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A.$" :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/68/6812e8036df171e162bee49d2edcff6d4a742e7bb4f14247713bd2332c64ccc6.png)

 

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq y  \leq 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^3\!-\!4y \bigg\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y  \leq 1, \quad 2y^3\!-\!2y \leq x \leq 0 \bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{3}-4y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2y-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}-2{y}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0}+{[{y}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129616 :question/id #uuid "4267a45d-477c-5267-95c7-1da5f4e02116" :question/math-academy-id "q-37760" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129192 :knowledge-point/id #uuid ![](images/33/33a38da74b282f0ec1fb2fae9cb155feb2a5fd39128c7607b80c6b84fedd29b4.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,x-1\le y\le 3-x}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,3-x\le y\le x-1}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{x-1}^{3-x}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{3-x}^{x-1}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{x-1}^{3-x}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{3-x}^{x-1}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[(3-x)^{2}-(x-1)^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}[(x-1)^{2}-(3-x)^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(8-4x)\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}(4x-8)\text{d}x \\  & =(8x-2{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{2}+(2{x}^{2}-8x){|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =8(2-1)-2({2}^{2}-{1}^{2})+2({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})-8(4-2) \\  & =8-6+24-16 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268866 :question/id #uuid "147c6c88-ba8a-5b9e-bbac-4eb8f1f8b260" :question/math-academy-id "q-132490"} {:db/id 17592186323935 :question/id #uuid "1e162c6a-7b02-5223-a553-b91cdf5010fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-37767" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129192 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4aa355fd-5d73-5cce-9c76-1edafae19751" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Partitioned Region"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2685a435-3b0b-5556-928d-8890e89f39c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{51}{4}" :db/id 17592186321449} {:answer/id #uuid "85db0642-7d1c-5c8d-a791-5339d42f6b66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{61}{5}" :db/id 17592186322209} {:answer/id #uuid "c2d61461-1e0a-5e92-8afb-016303b4ade2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{81}{6}" :db/id 17592186322658} {:answer/id #uuid "c6ee0989-2908-5bfb-9f66-c112c2783214" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{71}{3}" :db/id 17592186322689} {:answer/id #uuid "e9bcd73f-4f44-5e3e-887d-09a600ad1503" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{41}{6}" :db/id 17592186322976}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c6ee0989-2908-5bfb-9f66-c112c2783214" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{71}{3}" :db/id 17592186322689} :answer-field/id #uuid "07f87830-aaf6-5bb1-abec-9ce4771189f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186323181}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/8d/8de0dad0436135ef40aa26666d10659f4041275a915de153b6b4b45312c1c52f.png)

Evaluate ${∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\,dA,$ where $D$ is the region shown in the picture above." :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into three type II regions ${D}_{1},$ ${D}_{2},$ and ${D}_{3},$ as shown below.

![](images/b5/b58fc3909d5be467999053336f67d41b88b43c984208c60f3d46ee8b7479df58.png)

As a result, we get 

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,-2\le x\le -1},
$$

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le x\le 2}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{3}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,-2\le x\le 2}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}{x}^{2}y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}{x}^{2}y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{3}}{x}^{2}y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{y\text{ }\,{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{-1}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{y\text{ }\,{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{y\text{ }\,{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7y}{3}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7y}{3}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{16y}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot \frac{7}{3}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}+\frac{16}{3}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =\frac{71}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351404 :question/id #uuid "d3abb825-5e1f-5f44-b3d6-edf93dd36e5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-82223"} {:db/id 17592186351405 :question/id #uuid The region $D$ is enclosed by the the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=|x|,$ as shown in the picture. Evaluate ${∬}_{D}2x\,dA.$" :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/2f/2fcb30778db2f051a7a819ae701808af59ac18d27c25a9c57ce678caa6c3ee3b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le -x}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x}.
$$

 

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2x\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2x\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2x\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2x[-x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2x[x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(-2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{-1}^{0}+{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =((0-(-\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{4}))+((\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{4})-0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351419 :question/id #uuid "46c81894-7275-5b32-b94a-f373714d0ee2" :question/math-academy-id "q-82362" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129192 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4aa355fd-5d73-5cce-9c76-1edafae19751" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Partitioned Region"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "118a2340-ee04-5e42-8b78-10f4638b24da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "112" :db/id 17592186348600} {:answer/id #uuid "6749ded2-5b58-5631-9b85-8ecb08f12ff2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "44" :db/id 17592186349394} {:answer/id #uuid "858a7d1d-a35e-5216-9b5a-1f3b7e4c84e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "77" :db/id 17592186349667} {:answer/id #uuid "d3441c4c-6a81-5d07-9863-30030a1ac4f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{25}{6}" :db/id 17592186350302} {:answer/id #uuid "eb7751d6-cf40-59f1-9635-6dfff3b8fcc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186350502}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "858a7d1d-a35e-5216-9b5a-1f3b7e4c84e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "77" :db/id 17592186349667} :answer-field/id #uuid "e929c9d6-0a89-5b39-8782-8590a74cb865" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186351119}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/13/13275042f8b7b74e394b3cee1350c19cfa50ddf63899066682cbd0109f42d6bf.png)

Evaluate ${∬}_{D}4xy\,dA,$ where $D$ is the region shown in the picture above." :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/64/648121ff2a676f6a472a6e221dffe813eca55f914aed0ca9a285bb0d4cd81ab3.png)

   

As a result, we get 

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le 3},
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 3}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}4xy\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}4xy\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[2x{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}{[2x{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2x(9-1)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}2x(9-0)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}16x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}18x\,\text{d}x \\  & =8{x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{2}+9{x}^{2}{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =8(4-0)+9(9-4) \\  & =77.\end{aligned}

"First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-x & \,⟹\,x=-y \\ y=6-4x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4} \\ y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/08/08237d1ca2e01d0cf620dfa06a4265d8053b7ee34d0b65036aad7d5734726e1c.png)

 

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/c7/c756dc7924fc4c116601da907eb3b767b8a40647e063c146dad83b0ea660933b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y/2}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351394 :question/id #uuid "96fc8cbf-3b1e-5dd2-9a47-105985216141" :question/math-academy-id "q-82135" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129194 :knowledge-point/id #uuid Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions." :question/worked-solution "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={e}^{x} & \,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,x={e}^{y} \\ y=1+e-x & \,⟹\,x=1+e-y \\ y=1-x & \,⟹\,x=1-y\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/4d/4df7cf2f33520a80270341d4a40b4a83d9f3c11ed8adb69fe1131a42bcd61d5a.png)

    

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1-y\le x\le {e}^{y}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le e,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡y\le x\le 1+e-y}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-y}^{{e}^{y}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}^{1+e-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

$y=\sqrt{x-2}+1,$ and the lines $y=2-\frac{1}{2}x$ and $y=8-2x.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions." :question/worked-solution "First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\sqrt{x-2}+1 & \,⟹\,x=(y-1)^{2}+2 \\ y=2-\frac{1}{2}x & \,⟹\,x=4-2y \\ y=8-2x & \,⟹\,x=4-\frac{1}{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/3f/3f8e3ccfeac236d7fe9a502f599c61c404607a55ae809ec142019a3f881e1568.png)

  

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/31/3148cb0f499564db9cbfd6b635fef81dc47298789241af4a243c32dbf4dc8247.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,4-2y\le x\le 4-\frac{1}{2}y}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,(y-1)^{2}+2\le x\le 4-\frac{1}{2}y}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{4-2y}^{4-y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{(y-1)^{2}+2}^{4-y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048986 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428531 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency.
